newsitem.title: USA: Motorola outlook bright but cautious.
newsitem.headline: Motorola outlook bright but cautious.

text.p: Technology giant Motorola Inc said Wednesday its second-half outlook is bright, but not without warning about growing expenses in its planned satellite communications network and possible charges in other business segments.
"It's definitely an improving story," said Ajay Diwan, an analyst for Standard & Poor's equity group. "I think they're making great steps."
Motorola on Tuesday reported second quarter earnings of $0.62 a share, excluding a $170 million pretax charge, on revenues of $7.5 billion.
That easily topped analysts' expectations and exceeded year ago results, driving Motorola shares to a high of 86-7/8. On Tuesday, Motorola stock topped $80 for the first time in two years.

In a conference call with analysts on Wednesday, Motorola said overall orders in the second quarter rose 27 percent from last year, with key semiconductor products and cellular product orders up 36 percent and 20 percent respectively.
"The order strength there is encouraging to investors," said Robert Wilkes, an analyst with Brown Brothers Harriman.
And various new digital phone products are scheduled to ship during the second half, many in the third quarter.

But Motorola reduced its growth estimate for the worldwide semiconductor industry to six to eight percent for the year versus the 10 percent it forecast after the first quarter. The company attributed some tightening to the strong U.S. dollar.
Analysts pointed out that the company expects U.S. paging operators to keep tight controls on inventories, likely into 1998.

Motorola said future charges are possible as Motorola reviews its businesses which have not met expectations. The second quarter charge pays for its exit from a struggling dynamic random access memory (DRAM) market.

Motorola said digital phones made up 54 percent of handset sales, up from 37 percent for all of 1996. Up significantly were sales of Global System for Mobile Communication (GSM) technology, used largely in Europe, and Motorola said its GSM market share is increasing.
Motorola said it expects expenses associated with its 21 percent investment in Iridium LLC to be about $65 million in 1997 and "several times greater" than that in 1998.
Countering the expense and risk involved in building a global satellite communications network are the potential rewards of additional phone sales and increased semiconductor demand, analysts said.
Motorola's new chief executive Christopher Galvin has been a driver behind the satellite systems. In addition to Iridium, Motorola also plans to build two other networks.
"How that (satellite systems business) does will be one of the report cards that investors will be looking at 10 years from now," Wilkes said. "That's one of (Galvin's) key early decisions."
